title: How Miniature Golf Works
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the history of miniature golf from the 1867 Ladies Putting Club at St Andrews in Scotland, through James Barber's Thistle Dhu course in Pinehurst, North Carolina, the 1920s Tom Thumb Golf craze started by Garnet Carter and Thomas McCullough Fairbanks (spelled Fairburn in transcript), the rinky dink knockoffs of the Depression era, Don Clayton's putt putt courses in Fayetteville, North Carolina in 1954, the Lomas' mechanized windmill and clown-mouth courses, the 1990s return of professional golfers and competitions, and notable courses such as Myrtle Beach volcano courses, Parking in Lincolnshire Illinois, and Golf Gardens on Catalina Island. The episode closes with a listener mail about a family's road trip listening to the show.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

entities.name: Ladies Putting Club of St Andrews

segments.title: Book plug and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh promotes the upcoming book, then he and Chuck chat about their childhood memories of playing putt putt and miniature golf and their fondness for go karts.

segments.title: Ladies Putting Club and the first miniature course
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 1867 Ladies Putting Club course at St Andrews, built for women after a rule barring them from full swings, and explain that it was a golf course shrunk down. They discuss par three, pitch and putt, and executive courses.

segments.title: Spread to America: Thistle Dhu and the name miniature golf
segments.summary: James Barber built an eighteen-hole course called Thistle Dhu at his Pinehurst, North Carolina estate, the first in the United States. A newspaper account of competitions there coined the term miniature golf, which had earlier been called Lilliputian golf.

segments.title: 1920s rooftop courses and Tom Thumb Golf
segments.summary: A 1920s boom saw rooftop miniature courses in New York, and Garnet and Frieda Carter at Lookout Mountain's Fairyland Club built Tom Thumb Golf with fairy-tale obstacles tied to Rock City. Thomas McCullough Fairburn's cheap cottonseed-hull putting green made franchising possible.

segments.title: Miniature golf as a 1920s craze and Depression-era staple
segments.summary: Commerce Department figures suggest up to 25,000 courses in the US, many built in a few months. The craze faded but miniature golf stayed popular through the Depression, and cheap rinky dink knockoff courses built from found materials spread, with New York having about 150.

segments.title: Don Clayton and the birth of putt putt
segments.summary: In 1954, Don Clayton of Fayetteville, North Carolina, wanted a more skillful version without clowns and windmills. He built a course with about fifty dollars, and the name putt putt came from a bank paperwork mix-up over the spelling of Shady Veil. The company grew to about 256 courses, and it had a roller skating trail nearby.

segments.title: Windmills, clown mouths and mechanized courses
segments.summary: Ralph and Al Lomas of Scranton, Pennsylvania introduced moving windmills, ramps and other mechanized obstacles, creating modern goofy golf. Their components sold widely. The hosts note the evolution happened twice.

segments.title: Pro miniature golf and famous courses
segments.summary: In the 1990s professional golfers such as Jack Nicklaus got involved, with US Pro Mini Golf Association competitions and the World Mini Golf Sports Federation. The hosts discuss Myrtle Beach's mini golf strip, Al Graham Acres funeral home course, the Kiss-themed course in Las Vegas, Parking in Illinois, Golf Gardens on Catalina Island, and Florida's historic courses.

segments.title: Listener mail from Marabeth
segments.summary: A listener describes sharing the show with her parents on a road trip, and her dad's mixed-up name for the show. She also notes the fractals episode is nap-inducing in her family.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the show's email contact and close the episode.
